(AP) â Much of the U.S. is facing foul weather for Thanksgiving, with a storm in the East forcing the postponement of Macyâs 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade and strong winds and king tides prompting flood warnings and knocking out part of a city pier in the West.

The strengthening storm along the Eastern Seaboard raised worries about how the annual parade’s massive balloons would fare in the wind-swept canyons between Manhattanâs skyscrapers. Macy’s remarked in a statement that it was postponing the event until Saturday in an abundance of caution after consulting with city officials.

High winds, heavy rains and flooding plagued both coasts, complicating holiday travel, though the days leading up to Thanksgiving are typically far busier on the roads and in the airports than the holiday itself.

The storm was expected to hamper air travel at eastern U.S. airports Thanksgiving Day into Friday morning, with reduced visibility, greater turbulence, strong winds and aircraft icing, the National Weather Service said.

Wind gusts were expected to hit 50 mph (80 kph) or higher along the Interstate 95 corridor. The weather service posted wind advisories from northern Georgia to most of the mid-Atlantic to southern Latest England. All of New Jersey was under a state of emergency, declared by Gov. Mikie Sherrill on Wednesday night, as were parts of New York, following a declaration from Gov. Kathy Hochul.

Sources indicate that the storm was flooding coastal villages and cities from North Carolina through New Jersey as the high tide rolled in Thursday morning. Roads were closed and emergency workers were rescuing people from cars stranded in water.

Highways were shut down. The nearly 18-mile (29-kilometer) Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel in Virginia over the Chesapeake Bay was closed for several hours Thursday morning because of high winds. NC 12, the only highway connecting Hatteras Island on the North Carolina Outer Banks to the mainland was closed after seawater breached the dunes again and covered the two-lane highway. Crews did not know when it might reopen.

The Margate City Fire Department near Atlantic City, New Jersey, posted a video on Facebook of water pouring through the cityâs streets on a gray day where the heavy rains hadnât started yet.

A firefighter there said the tide was coming in ferociously and it was still an hour before its peak. Water closed in on steps to houses, and businesses had sandbags piled in front of their doors. When a reporter called looking for more information, the fire chief said he would have to call back because they had just been called to a fire.

In a recent development, winter storm warnings and watches were posted for parts of Missouri and Illinois, with up to 13 inches (33 centimeters) of snow expected around St. Louis by Thursday afternoon.

In a recent development, king tides continued surging on the West Coast, with coastal flood warnings issued from Southern California to the San Francisco area to the Oregon and Washington coasts. King tides occur when the gravitational pulls of the moon and sun align to raise water levels. Their effects this year are being amplified by the ongoing super El NiÃ±o, which has warmed the ocean, leading to an increased volume of seawater.

In a recent development, A video indicated a massive wave tearing down a portion of the pier in the city of Pacifica, California, on Wednesday and slamming it into the ocean. Officials had closed the L-shaped pier in the summer after finding cracks in the structure.

It has been revealed that north of San Francisco, Marin County officials issued an evacuation warning for residents of beachfront properties in Stinson Beach, saying large waves expected through the afternoon could send water and debris into roads and homes. The warning was lifted later Wednesday but authorities advised people to stay away from the beach as large waves continue to pound the area.

#135849. Refugees, asylum, and Supreme Court exceptionalism

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2117 w)

Refugees, asylum, and Supreme Court exceptionalism

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2117 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that american exceptionalism, the idea that the United States is uniquely virtuous, has deep roots that predate the nation itself.
  • It has been revealed that at best, American exceptionalism can be beneficent in intent and beneficial in result.
  • And then there is the Supreme Court’s wariness toward international law.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that american exceptionalism, the idea that the United States is uniquely virtuous, has deep roots that predate the nation itself. The founders of Latest England, in words echoed by President Ronald Reagan, famously declared that it was to be “as a citty upon a Hill. The eies of all people are upon us.”.

It has been revealed that at best, American exceptionalism can be beneficent in intent and beneficial in result. In time the New England states would become leaders in the abolition of slavery. Closer to our time, the United States would translate its victory in the Second Word War into the Marshall Blueprint, the World Bank, and the currently embattled international legal order under the aegis of the United Nations. The 18th Amendment, the juvenile death penalty (until 2005), and the failure to guarantee a right to healthcare furnish examples of exceptionalism gone wrong.

And then there is the Supreme Court’s wariness toward international law. At the Founding and for decades thereafter, the court tended to embrace “the law of nations,” either as a guide to interpreting relevant statutes or even as furnishing a rule of decision in appropriate circumstances. In more recent times, however, majorities have balked at viewing treaties as self-executing, taking guidance from the International Court of Justice, or applying statutes that expressly incorporate “the law of nations” into domestic law.

A grant of certiorari just this month will likely confirm the trend. The case is Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, in which the justices will review one of the Trump administration’s earliest attempts to restrict immigration. On the administration’s first day, a presidential proclamation declared that “an invasion is ongoing on the southern border.” The proclamation, among other things, sought to suspend entry to the United States for non-citizens “engaged in the invasion,” even for refugees fleeing persecution and seeking to apply for asylum. But the edict went one step further. It also mandated expedited removal to asylum seekers who had crossed the border seeking to apply for asylum and provided for expedited removal of such persons.

It has been revealed that the proclamation was issued notwithstanding a congressional framework that seeks to facilitate asylum – indefinite lawful residence – to those escaping persecution in their home country, set forth primarily in the 1952 Immigration and Nationality Act as amended by the 1980 Refugee Act and later amendments (codified under Title 8 of the U.S. Code). This framework: a) ensures a right to apply for asylum, b) links eligibility for asylum to refugee status, and c) provides protections against the government removing persons who would be likely to face persecution or torture.

In a recent development, section 1158 establishes the right to seek asylum. It provides that “[a]ny alien who is physically present in the United States … irrespective of such alien’s status, may apply for asylum.” The same section makes eligibility for asylum conditional, among other things, on a demonstration of refugee status. For this the statute relies on the definition of refugee in section 1101(a)(42) as a person who is unwilling or unable to return to their home country “because of persecution or a well-founded fear of persecution on account of race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion.”.

In a recent development, in turn, safeguards from removal come from two sources. The immigration statute itself states that noncitizens cannot be removed to a country where the attorney general determines that the “alien’s life or freedom would be threatened in that country because of the alien’s race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion.” In addition, the Foreign Affairs Reform & Restructuring Act of 1998 restricts removal to a country when “there are substantial grounds for believing the person would be in danger of being subjected to torture.”.

The Trump administration initially justified the denial of asylum and removal protections to those within the United States by invoking the president’s authority to suspend entry “of any aliens or of any class of aliens into the United States [that] would be detrimental to the interests of the United States.” The logic is that no one who violated the suspension by entering should be entitled to asylum and removal protections. To this defense the administration has added the formal role of the attorney general and director of Homeland Security. The INA grants each official the authority to grant asylum to eligible applicants as well as withhold removal for those who qualify. At the same time, the statute makes clear that these decisions are subject to individualized judicial review under an “abuse of discretion” standard. (At least until the second Trump administration, decisions not to grant relief to those who had demonstrated that they had qualified for asylum were the “exceedingly rare“ exception.).

Sources indicate that the lower courts rejected both justifications. Judge Randolph Moss of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia dismissed the administration’s claim that the president’s suspension of entry to those “engaged in [the] invasion” invalidated asylum and removal protections that expressly applied to persons physically in the country. The D.C. Circuit agreed with a slightly different emphasis. Writing for the majority, Judge Michelle Childs also rejected the idea that a suspension of entry justified eliminating asylum and removal safeguards for those present in the United States. To this point she added that, as a grant of asylum is discretionary, the express right to apply it entails individualized consideration rather than blanket elimination. (Judge Justin Walker issued a partial dissenting argument that the grant of discretionary authority permits a blanket denial of asylum claims.).

Industry observers note that the D.C. courts’ holdings are not wrong so far as they go. Suspending entry would appear to be a different power from removing someone after they had entered. The provisions for asylum strongly imply individualized consideration and even suggest a presumption of granting asylum to those who meet the detailed eligibility requirements. The relevant provisions plainly bar removal of those who qualify for that protection. But whether this reasoning will be sufficient at the Supreme Court is another matter. This is so not least given the justices’ recent penchant for giving the executive wide latitude on immigration.

But the justices should take into account some additional perspective.

Industry observers note that one relevant perspective comes from international law. Surprising as it may seem, the United States is not exceptional in having to grapple with immigration, refugees, and asylum. More surprising still, these common global challenges has yielded what should be familiar, common legal standards that apply, and to a great extent which owe their development to, the United States. Perhaps most surprising of all, standard domestic doctrines invite reference to this body of law when interpreting applicable federal statutes.

Consider first asylum. As an initial matter, the domestic asylum framework incorporates international standards as a function of congressional intent. As the court itself recognized in 1987’s INS v. Cardozo-Fonseca, Congress enacted the Refugee Act of 1980 to bring U.S. law in conformity with the nation’s obligations as a state party to the 1967 Protocol to the 1951 Refugee Convention. Crucially, in determining those obligations, the court sensibly drew upon the views of the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Refugees.

What do those obligations contemplate? The Refugee Conventions do not expressly provide for a right to apply for long-term asylum, as opposed to specifying rights for refugees fleeing persecution. But the UNCHR has maintained that international law presupposes individualized consideration of refugee status, especially before that status is denied. Given that Congress made the requirements for refugee status the basis for being eligible for asylum, it would be odd to conclude that the U.S. would remain in conformity with the convention as interpreted by the UN’s most authoritative body should the executive reject the right to seek asylum by means of a categorial denial of all asylum claims.

In a recent development, not surprisingly, categorical rejection of asylum claims would also be at variance with widespread international practice, especially as mandated in Europe. And neither last nor least, the administration’s position would also be inconsistent with the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights’ express guarantee of a right to asylum. Though not binding, the UDHR was adopted without dissent by the UN General Assembly, reflects the dominant position of the Member States, and informs their practice.

The Charming Betsy canon leads to the same conclusion. In the 1804 case Murray v. the Schooner Charming Betsy, Chief Justice John Marshall famously stated that “an act of Congress ought never to be construed to violate the law of nations if any other possible construction remains.” Marshall’s reference to the “law of nations” is generally understood to apply to modern customary international law. International custom arises given a near consensus of state practice perused out of a sense of legal obligation.

Section 1158’s grant of authority to the executive to grant asylum applications can be construed at least in two ways. It might mean a complete categorical discretion to deny. Or it might be better understood to assume individualized consideration. The latter clearly better comports with international practice. Yet there is even a stronger consideration. Customary, and for that matter treaty law, clearly prohibits removal to countries where a refugee has a well-founded fear of facing persecution or torture. When the result is expedited removal, the categorical denial of asylum status to persons claiming to escape from persecution and torture places the U.S. in obvious jeopardy of violating exactly this well-established international prohibition.

Sources indicate that which brings up the matter of removal itself. Here the upshot of Congress’ intent is more direct. Article 33.1 of the 1951 Refugee Convention provides: “No Contracting State shall expel or return (“refouler”) a refugee in any manner whatsoever to the frontiers of territories where his life or freedom would be threatened on account of his race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion.” Likewise, Article 3.1 of the Convention Against Torture mandates that “No State Party shall expel, return ("refouler") or extradite a person to another State where there are substantial grounds for believing that he would be in danger of being subjected to torture.” As noted, the Refugee Act in the first instance sought to place the U.S. in conformity with the Refugee Convention. FARRA sought to do the same with CAT. Categorically removing persons in the U.S. seeking asylum all but guarantees violations of the treaties that Congress sought to uphold.

So strong is the congressional intent argument that the Charming Betsy need not set sail. Yet even if the relevant statutory provisions were somehow ambiguous, the Charming Betsy canon would compel rejection of the administration’s position. Assume that section 1182(f), which grants the executive discretion to deny asylum claims, authorizes a categorial denial of applications across the board. Assume further that this section, along with section 1185(a)(1), can be read to permit removal of persons within the United States denied the opportunity to apply for asylum on the basis of persecution or torture. Even without the conventions, international practice has separately established “non-refoulement” – the prohibition of returning, or “refouling,” a person to return to a territory where he may be exposed to persecution as a matter of binding customary international law. Reading the relevant statutes to permit removal would then constitute a clear violation of non-refoulement. That reading would therefore also run counter to the Charming Betsy canon.

It has been revealed that A sad yet likely irony is that Mullin v. RAICES will privilege one strand of American exceptionalism over another. Much of the international law relevant to the case reflects the nation’s exceptional effort to leverage its dominance after the Second World War not to establish a traditional empire, but to construct a rules-based international order. One of many achievements was the 1951 Refugee Convention, like the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, brought about in no small part thanks to the efforts of Eleanor Roosevelt as a U.S. representative to the UN. Against this is the view that America has little to heed from the rest of the world, including on matters that implicate international affairs. The court adopted this stance on immigration as recently as last term. We shall see which view prevails.

Martin Flaherty is Charles and Marie Robertson Visiting Professor at the School of Public and International Affairs at Princeton, and Leitner Family Professor Chair of International Human Rights Law at Fordham Law School in New York.

Tech Report: Judge doesn’t like your objections? Here are some tips to keep them coming in a meaningful way

📅 30 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1093 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Abajournal

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Porto gets calls all the time from lawyers or litigants who want to appeal a verdict from a case that went horribly wrong.
  • Sometimes the problem is a bad jury instruction.
  • Porto, who specializes in appellate civil complications, wants to be able to deliver good news, but it’s not always possible, particularly if the attorneys failed to object in proper, timely way.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Juli M. Porto gets calls all the time from lawyers or litigants who want to appeal a verdict from a case that went horribly wrong.

Sometimes the problem is a bad jury instruction. Sometimes it’s a devastating ruling on key evidence. Sometimes the concern is the judge’s failure to stop opposing counsel from badgering a witness.

Porto, who specializes in appellate civil complications, wants to be able to deliver good news, but it’s not always possible, particularly if the attorneys failed to object in proper, timely way.

A principal at Blankingship & Keith in Fairfax, Virginia, Porto warns that typically, no matter how “egregious a trial judge’s error was, if it’s not preserved, it can’t be appealed.”.

Recent findings suggest that litigators know they need to preserve the record during court hearings, depositions or trial. And they’re aware that they generally can’t raise an objection for the first time on appeal.

But still, even the most experienced lawyers hesitate on how much to object and how far to go when advocating for their clients, particularly when judges appear to lose their patience.

According to recent reports, “It can be a delicate balance,” states J.C. Lore III, director of trial advocacy at Rutgers Law School. “Lawyers don’t want to make the judge angry.”.

Rule 103 of the Federal Rules of Evidence advises lawyers that objections must be timely and done with specificity.

While state rules of evidence vary, they tend to follow the same framework as the Uniform Rules of Evidence.

In addition, the American Bar Association Model Rule of Professional Conduct 1.1 requires lawyers to act competently.

Tiffany Williams Brewer is chair of the ABA Section of Litigation and a former Fresh Jersey state administrative law judge. She claims a lawyer’s role is to “courteously remind” the judge of the importance of preserving the record.

“As a former judge, I can relate that judges are often focused on the efficiency of moving the trial forward and may not even realize that they have skipped the opportunity to allow the lawyers to properly put their evidentiary basis on the record,” Brewer notes.

It has been revealed that most litigators have a war story or two where they felt they were being reasonable and advocating for their client while the judge was being unreasonable and obstructing them. And then there are the extreme cases.

In a Bexar County, Texas, court in 2024, then-Judge Rosie Speedlin Gonzalez accused an attorney of coaching her client and then pushed back when the attorney objected.

Gonzalez said the attorney was “not allowed to be argumentative and argue just for the sake of argument.”.

As the situation escalated, she ordered the attorney to be handcuffed and placed in the jury box.

Gonzalez was later charged over the incident, then the charges were dropped when she agreed to resign and never again seek reelection. She declined comment to the ABA Journal.

For the most part, Lore notes, judges know lawyers must make objections and don’t take it personally.

However, Lore says, when lawyers are using objections as a tactic to disrupt or rattle opposing counsel, judges tend to get angry and push back.

In a recent development, amy M. Stewart is a partner at Fisher Phillips in Dallas and chair of the ABA Section of Litigation.

“No one promised us in law school that making objections would be easy or without anxiety,” Stewart indicates.

Sometimes, dealing with a judge who won’t let counsel make proper objections requires some strategic maneuvering, she adds.

In one case, her firm hired an appellate lawyer to handle preserving the record during trial. Unfortunately, Stewart indicates, the judge told the appellate lawyer to “sit down” at critical moments in the trial.

“Appellate counsel held her own, but the drama was becoming distracting for the jurors,” Stewart states, so the trial team changed course, and had a male counsel make the objections.

“We realized the court never interrupted one of our co-lead counsels on the case,” Stewart indicates. “We coached him to make these critical objections, and the court would rule.”.

During his decades of litigation, Jules Epstein has seen all kinds of challenges come up during trial with judges who are reasonable and those who are less so. He suggests that if a judge is repeatedly blocking an attorney from making objections, the attorney should approach the judge calmly when the jury is not around.

“You can say to the judge, ‘I don’t want to violate your protocols, but I have to protect my client. Will you please give me instructions on how you want me to do this?’” claims Epstein, director of advocacy programs at Temple University Beasley School of Law.

If that doesn’t work, he says, a lawyer can file a written pleading or motion to preserve objections, including every single effort made to object in a timely way.

There’s also the option for an interlocutory appeal, depending on state rules, before a trial has concluded.

There are times, notes Ryan Watstein, that lawyers need to stand up to judges on behalf of their clients, even if that means they “catch a few black eyes” in the process.

“There are a lot of things culturally built into the practice of law, including a tendency to be intentionally hesitant to push back, particularly on the judiciary,” says Watstein, an Atlanta-based litigator and founding partner of Watstein Terepka.

Sources indicate that in a LinkedIn post in May, Watstein described how he was trying to convince a judge to rein in opposing counsel during discovery. Watstein kept arguing, and the judge yelled, “This is your last chance, Mr. Watstein.”.

Recent findings suggest that watstein explains that the courtroom was tense, and his client was uncomfortable. He thought he might get held in contempt.

In a recent development, “Every instinct our conservative profession teaches you was telling me to sit down,” Watstein indicates. “But I didn’t sit down.”.

According to recent reports, watstein claims he kept talking, despite the judge indicating it was time to stop. He said that he would seek appellate review of the judge’s decision if he didn’t get justice on the concern.

He ended up convincing the judge to reverse himself.

Watstein warns against being “overly deferential” when an “injustice is being perpetrated” against your client.

In a recent development, “You should always start in way that is respectful and professional, but there are circumstances where you have to push harder,” Watstein says. “The line that lawyers are trained to go up to is not necessarily the appropriate stopping point.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chinese Academy of Sciences researchers say the global water cycle has entered an âepoch of profound disruption.â.

(CN) â Global river flows and the amount of water held in lakes and reservoirs declined sharply during two years of exceptional heat, with freshwater resources falling to unprecedented levels in 2023 and 2024, researchers say in a new study published Thursday in Science.

According to recent reports, river discharge worldwide dropped 5.7% during the period, while active water storage in lakes and reservoirs fell 9.5% compared with the 1991-2020 average. The losses were particularly severe in South America, where river flows fell nearly 18%, even as some areas experienced heavy rainfall and flooding.

Led by Yongqiang Zhang, researchers at the Chinese Academy of Sciences examined global freshwater trends from 1991 through 2025, combining measurements from 150 major river basins with satellite observations of more than 1.2 million waterbodies.

Sources indicate that their analysis found that river flows and surface water storage fluctuated considerably between 1991 and 2006 before remaining relatively stable through 2022. Both measures then declined sharply in 2023 and 2024. River flows demonstrated signs of rebounding in 2025, but the researchers said the decline during the preceding two years was unprecedented in the historical record they examined.

South America was particularly hard hit. Streamflow fell 17.8%, while water held in lakes and reservoirs decreased 16.5%.

âThe global water cycle has already entered an Anthropocene epoch of profound disruption,â the researchers write.

The researchers linked the losses to the combined effects of two ocean climate patterns. El NiÃ±o, which develops in the Pacific Ocean, generally reduces rainfall across the Amazon. During the same period, unusually warm conditions in the tropical North Atlantic further disrupted the movement of moisture toward northern South America.

That combination intensified the region’s water shortages, even as other areas received enough rain to produce flooding.

Industry observers note that the findings show extreme heat can coincide with declining freshwater resources even in regions that typically receive abundant rainfall. Scientists have generally expected climate change to bring heavier precipitation to wet areas and increased evaporation in dry ones, but declining river flows and depleted soil moisture point to more complicated changes.

    Supreme Court defers decision on whether to dismiss major gun case

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (486 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, with just over a week remaining before the justices will hear oral argument in a pair of challenges to the constitutionality of bans on AR-15-style semiautomatic rifles, the Supreme Court on Tuesday afternoon put off a decision on a request by Cook County, Illinois, to dismiss the dispute over its ban as moot – that is, no longer a live controversy.
    • It has been revealed that the skirmish over whether the Illinois case should still go forward began on October 29, when Cutberto Viramontes, the named plaintiff in the case, filed a motion seeking to be dismissed from the case.
    • In a recent development, lawyers for Cook County subsequently asked the Supreme Court to dismiss the case as moot, arguing that it is “doubtful” that any of the other challengers would have a legal right to sue.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, with just over a week remaining before the justices will hear oral argument in a pair of challenges to the constitutionality of bans on AR-15-style semiautomatic rifles, the Supreme Court on Tuesday afternoon put off a decision on a request by Cook County, Illinois, to dismiss the dispute over its ban as moot – that is, no longer a live controversy. The court’s brief, unsigned order, which came one day after the justices granted a request by the lead plaintiff to remove him from the case, indicated that the justices would instead “defer[]” that ruling “pending oral argument,” which is scheduled for Wednesday, December 2.

    It has been revealed that the skirmish over whether the Illinois case should still go forward began on October 29, when Cutberto Viramontes, the named plaintiff in the case, filed a motion seeking to be dismissed from the case. Viramontes, who has been part of the challenge since it was filed in 2021, did not provide any explanation for his request.

    In a recent development, lawyers for Cook County subsequently asked the Supreme Court to dismiss the case as moot, arguing that it is “doubtful” that any of the other challengers would have a legal right to sue. They emphasized that Viramontes was a Cook County resident who said that he wanted to own an AR-15-style semiautomatic rifle. By contrast, they wrote, the other individual challenger in the case, Christopher Khaya, has said that he wants to own “an IMI Galil semiautomatic rifle,” which, according to Cook County, is not the kind of AR-15-style rifle covered by the question before the court.

    It has been revealed that the challengers countered that the question presented is not limited to AR-15 rifles but also extends to “similar” semiautomatic rifles, which would include AK-47-style rifles like the IMI Galil. But in any event, they added, Khaya “also desires to possess an AR-15 platform rifle and would acquire one if it were lawful for him to do so.”.

    Industry observers note that in its order deferring a decision on whether the Cook County case is moot because of the dismissal of Viramontes from the case, the Supreme Court cited its 2023 decision in Acheson Hotels, LLC v. Laufer, in which it unanimously agreed after oral argument that the case was moot because the plaintiff had voluntarily dismissed her lawsuit in the lower court. But the chances that the court will ultimately reach the merits of the ban are likely higher than in Acheson, in which there was only one plaintiff, because the dispute over semiautomatic rifles encompasses not only multiple plaintiffs but also another case – a challenge to Connecticut’s ban on AR-15-style rifles.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Mobile games compete with social media and streaming for attention in the cutthroat worlds of viral feeds and app marketplaces.

    • Industry observers note that people using apps like DoorDash and Uber, for instance, “have nothing to do while they wait,” as Braberg puts it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Mobile games compete with social media and streaming for attention in the cutthroat worlds of viral feeds and app marketplaces.

    Industry observers note that but wouldn’t it make more sense for these apps to compete for owners’ downtime? That’s the case made by Felix Braberg, a mobile ad and monetization consultant, in a blog post.

    Industry observers note that people using apps like DoorDash and Uber, for instance, “have nothing to do while they wait,” as Braberg puts it. Meanwhile, both DoorDash and Uber have billion-dollar annual ad businesses, but they’re not rushing to build their own gaming or streaming offerings. So they’re natural fits for app advertisers looking to help users pass the time.

    AppLovin’s strength in mobile gaming is not so dissimilar. But AppLovin has a nascent consumer advertising segment now, and a few of its early advertisers have noted the power of reaching people while they’re playing games on the toilet. It doesn’t get more “downtime” than that.

    It has been revealed that gaming can fit neatly into the downtime vacuum that right now is awkwardly filled by ads or nothing. But successfully advertising a mobile game traditionally required a user to download the game and leave the app where they saw it advertised.

    Industry observers note that now, though, startups such as PlaysOut are integrating mobile games directly into other apps and monetizing those experiences with rewarded video. It’s a way for nongaming apps to capitalize on the downtime that benefits gaming.

    Which leads Braberg to predict that the next wave of mobile growth “will come from apps that were never game companies.”.

    Scarcely a week after launching ChatGPT’s fresh Business Hub, designed to let businesses see how they’re performing in ChatGPT, OpenAI has revised the Hub’s terms of service, Digiday reports.

    The revisions came soon after Digiday reached out to OpenAI, citing legal concerns brought forward by lawyers on behalf of publishers.

    Some of those legal restrictions have been removed in the revised terms of service. However, the revised terms also introduced more restrictions, such as requiring companies to waive their right to seek a court order preventing OpenAI from using certain customer data.

    In a recent development, but, while OpenAI is still imposing some legal restrictions on companies that use its Business Hub, “they don’t leave a customer completely without recourse,” an IP and tech lawyer who requested anonymity tells Digiday. “A customer could still, even if not entirely practical, sue for monetary damages.”.

    The Italian conglomerate Bending Spoons has been amassing a collection of consumer- and business-facing software vendors that kind of resembles the Island of Misfit Toys. It added another dud (or stud?) to its stable last week.

    Bending Spoons will acquire Mailchimp from Intuit for about $3.7 billion, less than a third of what Intuit paid a decade ago, Reuters reports.

    Bending Spoons also recently added the online whiteboard Miro and location-based pet-tracking service Tractive, plus once-promising internet companies Brightcove, Evernote, Meetup, Vimeo and AOL. Its business model is akin to private equity, in that it acquires struggling companies and drastically reduces headcount while raising prices or removing free tiers. Interestingly, advertising is an ancillary part of its model.

    To be clear, AOL and Vimeo haven’t quit on ad revenue. But Bending Spoons is focused on subscription revenue growth and consolidated cost savings, rather than building an identity spine for advertising and data sales.

    In a recent development, but Bending Spoons still must demonstrate that it can turn flatlined businesses (Mailchimp declined year over year, for instance) into earners. Which is a bit like trying to bend a spoon using only your mind.

    Great news on the turnaround front: Bending Spoons reported 125% revenue growth last week.

    In a recent development, but there’s some not-so-great news, too: Its organic growth was an anemic 3%. So growth is coming from net-latest businesses, with these acquisitions contributing some $4 billion in debt.

    Apple is developing its own autonomous AI agents. [Bloomberg].

    Industry observers note that will Anthropic eventually launch an ads business? [Digiday].

    It has been revealed that the Nasdaq enters its third correction of 2026 amid a painful tech investor slide. [NYT].

    It has been revealed that A year in review of agency pitches. [Ad Age].

    Heading into the Thanksgiving break

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Happy Thanksgiving eve, SCOTUStoday readers!
    • In a recent development, following the Thanksgiving break, the court’s December argument session will begin, on Monday, November 30.
    • On Monday, the Supreme Court dismissed lead plaintiff Cutberto Viramontes from the case formerly known as Viramontes v.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Happy Thanksgiving eve, SCOTUStoday readers! We are very grateful for your support of our work. If you’d like to learn more about what the Supreme Court has noted about Thanksgiving, you can revisit our Closer Look on the topic from this time last year.

    In a recent development, following the Thanksgiving break, the court’s December argument session will begin, on Monday, November 30. The justices will hear eight total oral arguments during this session, addressing such problems as the Second Amendment, deportations to “third-party countries,” and the seizure of an airplane over the illegal transportation of beer.

    On Monday, the Supreme Court dismissed lead plaintiff Cutberto Viramontes from the case formerly known as Viramontes v. Cook County, on whether the Second Amendment guarantees a right to possess AR-15s and similar semiautomatic rifles, but it did not take action on Cook County’s request to dismiss the case as moot. On Tuesday, the court revealed that it had deferred action on that request until after oral argument, which will take place on Wednesday, December 2. The case name is now Khaya v. Cook County. For more on Tuesday’s announcement, see the On Site section below.

    The Supreme Court Building will be closed tomorrow and Friday for Thanksgiving.

    The December argument session will begin on Monday. That day, the justices will hear oral arguments in two cases: Crowther v. Board of Regents of the University System of Georgia, on whether Title IX, the federal law that prohibits sex-based discrimination by schools that receive federal funding, allows school employees to bring lawsuits alleging sex discrimination; and Wassily v. Blanche, on whether immigrants whose asylum protections have been terminated remain eligible to become lawful permanent residents, also known as green card holders.

    Recent findings suggest that on Tuesday, the justices will hear argument in Jouppi v. Alaska, an Alaskan bush pilot’s challenge to the forfeiture of his $95,000 airplane over the transport of beer into a dry village.

    On Wednesday, December 2, the court will hear argument in Khaya v. Cook County, on the constitutionality of bans on AR-15s and similar semiautomatic rifles, at 10:00 a.m. EST. As noted above, we will be live blogging that morning beginning at 9:30 a.m.

    Jack Birle, Washington Examiner.

    In June 2022, the Supreme Court ruled “in Carson v. Makin that Maine could not exclude religious schools from a state program that allows parents to use vouchers for public or private schools for their children.” Now, a group of Catholic schools has asked the justices to revisit the program and address rules that were passed while the earlier case was pending “to bar schools from participating ... if their admissions policies prefer students of a certain religion, allow religious discrimination in their schools, or do not follow the state’s views on gender ideology,” according to the Washington Examiner. “The Catholic schools urge the Supreme Court to address multiple questions if it takes up the case, including whether to overrule the 1990 Supreme Court ruling Employment Division v. Smith, which found that the free exercise clause does not allow for people to violate a law as part of their religious practice, as long as the law is valid and neutral in how it is applied. The petition ... argues that Smith has allowed Maine to continue to exclude religious schools from state programs.”.

    Attorneys for Emily Bickford, a Maine mother “who has been prohibited from taking her 13-year-old daughter to church” in a custody order, appealed her challenge to the order to the Supreme Court last week. The order allows the child’s father “to solely decide on his daughter’s involvement with Calvary Chapel Church.” Bickford asks the justices to find that it violates “parental rights and religious liberty protections,” according to WMTW in Portland, Maine. “A parent’s ability to take her child to church during her own parenting time now depends on the State in which she lives,” Bickford’s petition for review says. “When a state court strips a fit parent of her right to direct her child’s religious upbringing and vests a co-parent with veto power, it deploys the coercive authority of the State to extinguish a fundamental right.”.

    Kanishka Singh and Julia Harte, Reuters.

    On Tuesday, “Salvadoran migrant Kilmar Abrego Garcia, whose wrongful deportation to El Salvador made him a symbol for critics of President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, left the US for Spain,” according to Reuters. His voluntarily departure brought an end to “a legal fight that, at one point, reached the US Supreme Court.” It began when “US authorities sent Abrego Garcia, who entered the US illegally, to a megaprison in El Salvador in March 2025 despite a prior court order barring his return there because of the risk of persecution.” For months, officials “mentioned they could not bring him back,” but the Supreme Court ultimately “ordered the government [to] facilitate Abrego Garcia’s return.” After he returned to the United States in June 2025, Abrego Garcia faced human smuggling charges “stemming from an earlier incident” and a renewed deportation effort.

    Gavin Bade, The Wall Street Journal.

    Since February, when the Supreme Court held that President Donald Trump did not have the authority under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act to impose tariffs, the Trump administration has been using other statutes to rebuild the president’s tariff regime. This week, that effort will continue when the administration announces increased “tariffs on China and dozens of other countries,” according to The Wall Street Journal. “The new tariffs will likely be added to levies from a separate tariff action, unveiled in July, that sought to penalize nations for not blocking the trade of goods produced with forced labor,” and target countries that the Trump administration has concluded are harming U.S. producers by “flood[ing] global markets with cheaper goods.” That July action sparked a new lawsuit over the administration’s tariff policies.

    On Monday, a panel for the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit sided with President Donald Trump “in his fight to overturn his hush money criminal conviction in New York, ruling that a judge wrongly denied his effort to move the case into federal court,” according to The Hill. Trump’s current push to transfer the case “cites the Supreme Court’s presidential immunity ruling.” The president contends that “he has the legal right to bring it up before a federal judge as a defense,” and the 2nd Circuit panel held on Monday that the district court did not properly consider this argument. “Monday’s decision effectively puts a halt to Trump’s ongoing appeal in New York’s state court system and moves it to federal court, where the president will continue pressing his arguments that the case should remain there.”.

    Philip Jankowski, The Dallas Morning News.

    Sources indicate that texas’ Democratic Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson said he will not defend the state’s “Ten Commandments classroom law,” just weeks before the justices are expected to consider whether to take up a challenge to it, according to The Dallas Morning News. “My jurisprudential opinion is that the law is unconstitutional,” Johnson said. “The court will have the ultimate say as to what’s constitutional and what is not, but I’m the one who notes what the state’s position is, and it will not be the position the state has previously taken.” Outgoing Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton “cited Johnson’s unwillingness to defend the law as a reason the justices should decline to hear” the challenge to it in the state’s brief in opposition, which was filed on November 10. “If the Supreme Court stays out of the fight, a federal appeals court ruling upholding the classroom displays in Texas would remain in place, preserving a legal victory for Paxton even after he leaves office in January.”.

    Sources indicate that with just over a week remaining before the justices will hear argument in a pair of challenges to the constitutionality of bans on AR-15-style semiautomatic rifles, the Supreme Court on Tuesday afternoon put off a decision on a request by Cook County, Illinois, to dismiss the dispute over its ban as moot – that is, no longer a live controversy. The court’s brief, unsigned order came one day after the justices granted a request by the lead plaintiff to remove him from the case.

    Industry observers note that on Tuesdays for the past few months, we have dedicated the Closer Look section of this newsletter to covering the plaintiffs behind landmark Supreme Court cases. In this article, Blake took a step back and reflected on what we have learned.

    In his Empirical SCOTUS column, Adam Feldman analyzed each justice’s voting pattern in interim docket cases involving federal executive action, highlighting “a conservative majority whose members separate over particular exercises of federal power, a liberal bloc with distinguishable voting and dissent records, and occasional alliances that cross ideological lines.”.

    In a recent development, in his Court Beyond Borders column, Martin Flaherty focused on the Supreme Court’s grant of review in Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, on President Donald Trump’s suspension of asylum at the U.S.-Mexico border. The case, according to Flaherty, will put “the Supreme Court’s wariness toward international law” in the spotlight.

    Sources indicate that in her In Dissent column on Monday, Anastasia Boden explored 1978’s Federal Communications Commission v. Pacifica Foundation, holding that the government may “constitutionally prohibit indecency even” when it falls “short of legal obscenity.” In a dissenting opinion, Justice William Brennan criticized the majority for “attempt[ing] to impose its notions of propriety on the whole of the American people.”.

    (SCOTUSblog Plus) Since joining in 2022, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson has forged a unique role on the Supreme Court. It often appears, as Amy noted in this analysis, that Jackson’s goal in dissenting opinions is not simply to express disagreement with the majority, but to offer an alternative vision of the law and speak to the public directly – regardless of whether anyone else on the court agrees.

    In his SCOTUSCrim column on Friday, Rory Little aimed “to demonstrate that much of criminal law is actually constitutional law” and explore “why that can be so interesting.”.

    Sarah Isgur and David French critique Congress’ current governing processes with the help of Michael “Frags” Fragoso, a partner at Torridon Law, and Nicholas Bagley, a professor of law at the University of Michigan and author of the book Why We Can’t Have Nice Things: How Legal Reformers Accidentally Broke America.

    The Closer Look in Wednesday editions is typically an entry in our Ask Amy series, in which Amy Howe answers reader questions about the Supreme Court.

    According to recent reports, Q: At least for those of us of a certain age, the November 9 order list contained a familiar name in the “Attorney Discipline” section: Larry Klayman, perhaps best known as a frequent and fervent foe of the Clinton administration, had been “disbarred from the practice of law” in the Supreme Court. Which leads to the question: How, exactly, does someone get disbarred from the Supreme Court bar – especially if, like Klayman, they’ve never argued there?

    A: The answer (like so many others) can be found in the Supreme Court’s rules, starting with the rule that outlines how someone becomes eligible to join the Supreme Court bar, which is necessary not only to argue before the justices but also to sign filings there: lawyers must have been (among other things) “admitted to practice” in another jurisdiction for at least three years, and they cannot have been subject to any disciplinary proceedings during that time.

    In a recent development, because becoming a member of the Supreme Court bar requires a clean disciplinary record, it follows that disciplinary problems can get a lawyer kicked out of the Supreme Court bar – even if the underlying conduct had nothing to do with the court itself. Specifically, the court’s rules provide for the suspension of any lawyer who “has been disbarred or suspended from practice in any court of record, or has engaged in conduct unbecoming a member of the Bar of this Court.” The suspended lawyer then has the chance to try to persuade the court “why disciplinary action should not be taken,” after which the court may take “any appropriate disciplinary action,” which can include disbarment.

    According to recent reports, in Klayman’s case, he was apparently suspended by the bar associations in the District of Columbia and Florida for alleged ethical violations in connection with his efforts to represent rancher Cliven Bundy in a federal court in Nevada, leading to his disbarment from the Supreme Court earlier this month. Klayman told Law360 that he looks to seek reconsideration of the Supreme Court’s order.

    “It is like having a upcoming in-law at Thanksgiving dinner. Uncle Fred will put on a clean shirt.”.

    — Chief Justice John Roberts’ thoughts when a new member joins the Supreme Court.

    #135839. Latest Update: The Trade Desk Can Win Again By Embracing Objectivity And Letting Go Of The Open Web

    Latest Update: The Trade Desk Can Win Again By Embracing Objectivity And Letting Go Of The Open Web

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1054 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, wall Street loves to pile on ad tech.
    • No manufacturer has felt the highs and lows of being public quite like The Trade Desk (TTD), which, outside of AppLovin and the Magnificent 7, is the best company to emerge from the ad tech sector in the last 25 years.
    • It has been revealed that TTD was built on a brilliant principle: that brands and agencies should be able to decide where their media dollars go without the tech giant selling the media sitting in the room.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, wall Street loves to pile on ad tech. They’re all about you when you’re up and quick to dismiss you when you’re down.

    No manufacturer has felt the highs and lows of being public quite like The Trade Desk (TTD), which, outside of AppLovin and the Magnificent 7, is the best company to emerge from the ad tech sector in the last 25 years.

    It has been revealed that TTD was built on a brilliant principle: that brands and agencies should be able to decide where their media dollars go without the tech giant selling the media sitting in the room. That idea remains true, and it is the reason TTD became the largest independent DSP in the world.

    So what changed? TTD latched onto a new principle: the defense of the open internet. Which means the firm built its core value prop around a shrinking portion of where consumers spend their time and where advertisers spend their money.

    Sources indicate that as DV360 became Google’s Death Star, The Trade Desk was the Rebel Alliance standing up for the open web. But while TTD spent the last several years proving they were the anti-Google, Amazon snuck in the back door and changed the whole DSP market.

    If The Trade Desk holds to its first principle and lets go of the second, its value becomes more obvious than ever. Three moves would signal a upcoming era for the company:.

    Industry observers note that 1. Separate the value prop of “open internet” with objective decisioning. The manufacturer should retire the open internet as its stated purpose and replace it with what all advertisers value: independent, data-driven decisioning for brands and agencies. The open web stays in the portfolio as one channel among several, allowing buyers to see the whole field.

    It has been revealed that 2. Offer an objective view of the walled gardens. Google will not let a third-party DSP bid on YouTube, and Meta has shown no interest in opening its auction. But neither fact prevents The Trade Desk from ingesting platform reporting, independent measurement and content data from nearly every walled garden, then normalizing it against its own CTV and open web buys.

    3. Save the open internet by showing the whole picture. TTD taking an objective view of all platforms would highlight measurement and quality discrepancies. Which would, in turn, improve the open internet’s reputation in the eyes of the buy side. Without that full view, there is no way to show how “premium” open internet performs against the largest user-generated platforms in the world.

    In a recent development, from the beginning, The Trade Desk owned no inventory at all. It had no financial reason to steer a dollar anywhere except where the data mentioned it would work for the buyer.

    TTD’s 2016 S-1 organized the company’s strengths under headings like “We Do Not Arbitrage Advertising Inventory” and “We Are Data-Driven.” The phrase “open internet” does not appear in the company’s prospectus summary or risk factors at all.

    Recent findings suggest that the business built on that positioning worked extremely well. TTD went public in September 2016, grew revenue from $308 million in 2017 to $2.44 billion in 2024, reached a market cap of roughly $40 billion by 2021 and met or beat expectations for 33 consecutive quarters.

    In 2025, growth slowed and stock performance followed suit. That slowing growth is the natural effect of being the Pied Piper of the shrinking “open web.”.

    Redseer Strategy Consultants estimate that the programmatic open web gets only 20%-30% of ad budgets, with 70%-80% of programmatic spend going to walled gardens. This split has held for roughly five years.

    Recent findings suggest that advertisers have already made their decision. Budgets did not follow time spent, because walled gardens offer simplicity that programmatic cannot: an easy button for efficient reach. While the value of that reach can be debated, the easy way won.

    The concentration of spend is still increasing. EMarketer expects Google, Meta and Amazon to take 62.3% of worldwide digital ad spend in 2026, with Meta at about $243 billion and Google at about $240 billion. Amazon is forecast to grow from $69 billion in 2025 to $97 billion in 2027. Every incremental dollar in those forecasts is a dollar that an independent DSP cannot bid on today. Forecasts are growing faster than the open web.

    Television was supposed to be the market where the “open internet” reclaimed ground with upper-funnel brands. Except CTV is also becoming a walled garden medium. In Nielsen’s May 2026 Gauge, YouTube accounted for 13.8% of all US TV viewing, making Google the single largest media distributor in the US.

    Recent findings suggest that advertisers have limited transparency into the AI products of each walled garden. The content itself is UGC (and increasingly AI-generated). The measurement is dictated by the platform. And yet marketers need to spend there in order to get reach and efficiency. Imagine if there were a truly objective way to spend those dollars?

    Sources indicate that none of this means that TTD’s founding principle failed. It means the principle is aimed at an open web target that keeps getting smaller. An objective buyer that can only see 20%-30% of the budget is no longer willing to spend the time, money and energy on the shrinking pie.

    In a recent development, CMOs have one budget. The question they actually want answered is where the next dollar should go across YouTube, Meta, TikTok, Snap, CTV and the web, backed by objective data. Today, nobody independently answers that question. The Trade Desk is the only firm in the industry that is poised to provide a solution.

    Industry observers note that most turnarounds require a organization to find a newly introduced reason to exist, and most of them fail because the new reason is never as convincing as the original one. This turnaround just requires The Trade Desk to remember its original reason for being.

    When The Trade Desk opens up its view beyond the open web, Wall Street – and the buy side – will rejoice.

    “Data-Driven Thinking” is written by members of the media community and contains fresh ideas on the digital revolution in media.

    #135837. AI Needs To Cite Its Sources. This Consumer Intelligence Platform Ensures It Does

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (697 w)
    📖 Baca

    AI Needs To Cite Its Sources. This Consumer Intelligence Platform Ensures It Does

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (697 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When Stravito was released roughly nine years ago, its goal was to help brands put the right product in front of the right consumer early in their shopping journey.
    • In a recent development, now, in the age of generative AI, its focus hasn’t changed so much as its structure and execution.
    • At the crux of the firm is “the idea of bringing your strategy to life,” CEO and Founder Thor Olof Philogène told AdExchanger.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When Stravito was released roughly nine years ago, its goal was to help brands put the right product in front of the right consumer early in their shopping journey.

    In a recent development, now, in the age of generative AI, its focus hasn’t changed so much as its structure and execution. Stravito, which touts itself as a consumer intelligence platform, uses AI to help marketers better understand their customers’ preferences and predict their reactions to ads.

    At the crux of the firm is “the idea of bringing your strategy to life,” CEO and Founder Thor Olof Philogène told AdExchanger.

    Indeed, it’s the crux of the manufacturer name: Stravito is a portmanteau of the words “strategy” and “vito,” which comes from the Latin word for life, “vita.”.

    In September, it debuted its AI Persona Builder product, which uses brands’ data to develop AI personas that reflect their audiences.

    Sources indicate that stravito connects to a brand’s first-party data as well as other sources, like surveys and syndicated research, plus Stravito’s data from prior campaigns. From there, it builds out different AI personas for different audiences. The personas can represent smaller, more niche audiences, like people from a specific geo to capture “regional nuances,” mentioned Philogène, or broader audiences, like millennials or Gen Z. Marketers can ask a persona a specific question, like why they prefer one version of an ad over another, “and get instant feedback,” he added.

    According to recent reports, coffee brand Lavazza, for instance, conducted several thousand consumer interviews that it was able to integrate into the personas it built with Stravito. When Lavazza was testing different styles of packaging for its Dolcevita line of coffee, it was able to get feedback on the different variations from a relevant customer persona.

    For this particular launch, Lavazza tested its US audience persona, which was built on data, including roughly 5,000 consumer interviews conducted through Kantar and research by the National Coffee Association. The research “covered consumers’ broader attitudes toward life, not only their attitudes toward coffee,” mentioned Philogène, which helped with aesthetic decisions.

    In a recent development, based on the persona’s responses to the colors and other visual cues, Lavazza ultimately changed the packaging color from black to dark blue, Philogène remarked. It then validated the decision by testing the upcoming designs on Meta and comparing engagement.

    In a recent development, but rather than just spitting out recommendations and hoping that marketers will trust the personas’ responses at face value, Stravito takes a “glass box” approach to AI, said Philogène. This means that every suggestion and piece of feedback that the AI generates is accompanied by the specific sources and citations that informed it.

    When your boss asks why you’re making a certain investment, “you do not want to tell them, you know, because AI told me so,” quipped Philogène. Instead, Stravito backs up its decision with the data sources it’s connected to.

    In a recent development, but no matter how much research a brand or tech vendor has access to, no AI tool can accurately answer every question that someone may pose. And Stravito is exceedingly aware of that. Before a user even asks a question, said Philogène, the AI persona will note topics that it doesn’t have enough data to answer questions about, such as a brand’s pricing model.

    According to recent reports, an AI tool’s lack of knowledge can be “a feature, not a bug,” mentioned Philogène. It’s crucial for brands to understand what data they’re lacking and where they should commission extra data, he added.

    Recent findings suggest that stravito’s AI “won’t be sycophantic” and just tell customers what they want to hear, noted Philogène. (Take that, ChatGPT.) Rather, it first determines whether or not it has enough data to answer a given question, and if it does, it specifies whether the answer is explicitly stated in the original source versus inferred. That way, the user can understand the logic backing up every one of the model’s conclusions.

    Having the necessary sources to back up one’s claims and decisions is a crucial facet of journalism, law and research, Philogène remarked. Shouldn’t advertising be held to the same standard?

    Justices to consider whether noncitizens who lose asylum status may still obtain green cards

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1304 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that the Supreme Court on Monday will hear oral argument in Wassily v.
    • Although the case will almost certainly be overshadowed by many of this term’s other immigration disputes – including Mullin v.
    • The challengers in Wassily are two men who lost their asylum protections after being convicted of what immigration officials determined to be “particularly serious crime[s].”.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that the Supreme Court on Monday will hear oral argument in Wassily v. Blanche, a case on whether immigrants whose asylum protections have been terminated remain eligible to become lawful permanent residents, also known as green card holders.

    Although the case will almost certainly be overshadowed by many of this term’s other immigration disputes – including Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, on the Trump administration’s suspension of access to asylum for immigrants at the U.S.-Mexico border – it may hold considerable consequences for noncitizens and bring new significance to the Trump administration’s effort to scale back asylum.

    The challengers in Wassily are two men who lost their asylum protections after being convicted of what immigration officials determined to be “particularly serious crime[s].”.

    According to recent reports, tamer Wassily was granted asylum in 2000 after raising concerns about facing religious persecution in his home country of Egypt. The Department of Homeland Security moved to terminate Wassily’s asylum protections after he was convicted in 2004 of third-degree stalking and child endangerment, beginning the process of deporting him back to Egypt.

    Byron Velasquez Arreaga came to the United States from Guatemala in 1995 and was granted asylum the following year. After Velasquez Arreaga was convicted of driving while intoxicated in 2015 and for aggravated driving while intoxicated in 2018, DHS indicated that it would terminate his asylum protections and move to deport him.

    Sources indicate that amid their removal proceedings, and after their asylum protections had been terminated, both Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga applied to become lawful permanent residents. This option is available to asylum recipients who meet certain requirements, including remaining in the United States for at least a year after receiving asylum protections, under 8 U.S.C. § 1159(b).

    After many years of complicated legal wrangling before immigration judges and the Board of Immigration Appeals, the men’s cases were considered together by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit. The question before that court – and the question that is now before the Supreme Court – was whether noncitizens like Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga remain eligible for adjustment of immigration status under Section 1159(b) after their asylum protections have been terminated, because the statute refers to “any alien granted asylum” but is silent as to whether applicants must at the moment be asylees.

    In a 2-1 ruling, a 2nd Circuit panel rejected the men’s contention that “granted asylum” addresses a past decision – in which case anyone who had ever received asylum would be eligible for status adjustment under Section 11159(b) – and concluded that noncitizens whose asylum protections have been terminated are “categorically barr[ed]” from applying for adjustment to permanent legal status.

    Sources indicate that writing for the majority, Judge Richard Wesley emphasized the use of the word “status” in the opening of Section 1159(b), which reads: “The Secretary of Homeland Security or the Attorney General ... may adjust to the status of an alien lawfully admitted for permanent residence the status of any alien granted asylum.” According to Wesley, a “natural reading of ‘the status of any alien granted asylum’ is that a noncitizen must presently be granted asylum to adjust to lawful permanent resident status under 8 U.S.C. § 1159(b).”.

    Sources indicate that in January, Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga asked the Supreme Court to review the 2nd Circuit’s ruling, highlighting a disagreement between the federal courts of appeals over whether the phrase “granted asylum” in Section 1159(b) “refer[s] to a completed, historical event” or “a continuing, present status.” Like the 2nd Circuit, they noted, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit has held that noncitizens who have lost their asylum protections “are categorically ineligible” “for adjustment to [lawful permanent resident] status under Section 1159(b).” The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit, on the other hand, has held that such immigrants remain “eligible for adjustment.”.

    In late June, the justices granted review.

    In their brief on the merits, Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga contend that the 2nd Circuit’s decision is out of step with the “[t]ext, context, structure, history, and purpose” of Section 1159(b). In particular, they highlight several nearby passages in which lawmakers explicitly imposed “continuing conditions” that address a termination of immigration status, asserting that Congress “could have and would have” included such a condition here if it intended to unambiguously bar former asylees from applying for lawful permanent residency.

    The two men also point to Section 1159(c), which grants the DHS secretary and attorney general the authority to waive portions of the statute “for humanitarian purposes, to assure family unity, or when it is otherwise in the public interest.” Holding that adjustment to lawful permanent residency is categorically unavailable to noncitizens whose asylum protections have been terminated “would take core parts of that discretion away,” the men write. Such a limitation cuts against Congress’ purpose for allowing for discretion, Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga argue. “There are many reasons why Congress would want” these officials “to retain discretion” here, they say, including that termination sometimes stems from factors “entirely outside” an asylee’s control. For example, the immigration status of the spouse and children of an asylee is often linked to the asylee’s status. If the noncitizen who was originally granted asylum loses his or her status, so does the whole family.

    Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga ask the justices to recognize that, at the very least, the text of Section 1159(b) is unclear and to apply the rule of lenity, which they describe as a “well-settled and longstanding principle” under which “ambiguous provisions leading to the severe sanction of removal should be construed in favor of the noncitizen.” The Supreme Court “has repeatedly restated and reaffirmed that rule,” they conclude.

    Sources indicate that in its merits brief, the federal government counters that Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga’s interpretation of Section 1159(b) defies common sense. The text of the statute, according to U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer, describes a “transition from one status (that of an ‘alien granted asylum’) to another (that of an ‘alien lawfully admitted for permanent residence’).” If an immigrant is no longer at that starting point because his asylum status has been terminated, he can’t make the transition, Sauer asserts.

    The government contends that the “statutory context” supports this interpretation, because, in nearby passages, “alien granted asylum” clearly refers to a noncitizen’s “present status.” For example, in Section 1158(c)(1), “Congress identified benefits available to an ‘alien granted asylum,’ including protection from removal and work authorization,” according to Sauer. “Those benefits undisputedly cease when asylum status is terminated.”.

    According to recent reports, the government rejects the idea that barring noncitizens who have lost their asylum status from applying for a green card would interfere with the authority of the DHS secretary and attorney general to exercise discretion. Officials, Sauer writes, would remain free to intervene at an earlier point to prevent the termination of asylum status in the first place.

    Sources indicate that sauer concludes by urging the justices to reject what he characterizes as a “last-resort appeal to lenity” – that is, Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga’s claim that Section 1159(b) is an “ambiguous provision[]” and should therefore be interpreted in their favor. He argues that the rule of lenity does not apply here, not just because the meaning of the provision is clear, but also because Section 1159(b) does not directly address deportation, which is the context in which the rule of lenity arises.

    In a recent development, the Supreme Court’s decision in Wassily v. Blanche is expected by early July at the latest.

    Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

    OpenAI’s New Shopping Strategy; What Advertisers Are Thankful For

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sometimes, momentous change happens in the most banal ways.
    • So it was last week when OpenAI made an unheralded change to its “Shopping with ChatGPT Search” documentation, as AI Visibility Journal reports.
    • The documentation previously read: “Product results are selected independently by ChatGPT and are not ads, nor influenced by any OpenAI partnerships.” Now it reads: “Product results are not ads; how products and merchants are selected is described below.”.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sometimes, momentous change happens in the most banal ways.

    So it was last week when OpenAI made an unheralded change to its “Shopping with ChatGPT Search” documentation, as AI Visibility Journal reports.

    The documentation previously read: “Product results are selected independently by ChatGPT and are not ads, nor influenced by any OpenAI partnerships.” Now it reads: “Product results are not ads; how products and merchants are selected is described below.”.

    The cynical take is that OpenAI is now allowing room for marketing partnerships to influence ChatGPT’s product recommendations, even outside of official ads.

    Sources indicate that other changes to the documentation are less vital, though telling. ChatGPT formerly committed to showing products with “links to sites where you can learn more or purchase.” Now ChatGPT’s mandate is only to “show available ways to purchase.”.

    Marketers and merchants want to influence how their products and brands are presented to AI search customers. There’s massive demand for such services (which are called AEO or GEO, as an evolution of SEO).

    Industry observers note that plus, some platforms that are essential for AI training are monetizing their influence over the chatbots. Amazon recently rolled out “Conversational Briefs” – a silly underwear-adjacent name for a product that lets brands pay to affect relevant AI search outputs.

    But AI platforms themselves are hesitant to break the dam and let brands pay to boost their profile directly. Which could look like, for instance, businesses picking and choosing which customer reviews get surfaced or considered by the model, or pay-to-play prompts or keywords.

    Holiday ads might be creeping into the schedule earlier than ever this year, but don’t get it twisted: For a lot of TV advertisers, broadcasters and streamers, Thanksgiving weekend is the main event.

    On Thursday, NBCUniversal has the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, the National Dog Show and one of three Thanksgiving NFL games (CBS and Fox will broadcast the other two). Meanwhile, on Wednesday, Netflix has the first-ever Thanksgiving Eve NFL game, and Prime Video is airing its first Duke men’s college basketball game. Then, on Black Friday, Prime has a 15-hour marathon of live sports coverage lined up, including an NFL game, two Emirates NBA Cup games and a PGA golf event.

    Sources indicate that all that TV makes this weekend a crucial one for advertisers. Not only are many more people watching live during the Thanksgiving weekend (a record 34 million watched the Macy’s parade last year), but the National Retail Federation estimates that 182.7 million are planning to shop then, too.

    Which means it’s one of the rare times when TV is both a massive brand awareness play and short-term performance driver.

    It’s no wonder, then, that both NBC and Amazon are leaning heavily into interactive ad formats for their streaming broadcasts this year, as Variety reports. Amazon’s ads will feature on-screen prompts for interacting with Alexa or adding items straight to a customer’s Amazon cart, while Peacock will present shoppable pause ads that set up Instacart deliveries for users.

    Ruh-roh: Loads of ad dollars are still getting lost in the programmatic abyss.

    Only 43.1% of programmatic spend made it to “quality media” last quarter, according to the latest ANA Programmatic Transparency Benchmark report. The research claims that, for every $1 million of programmatic ad spend, more than half is lost to transaction costs ($285,000) and media productivity ($284,000).

    Ad tech taxes aren’t solely to blame for the wasted spend, though. The lack of effective measurement is also a significant source of programmatic inefficiency, according to the ANA. And poor measurement standards are a “particularly acute” problem in connected TV environments, where a whopping 24% of ad spend went to “non-measurable inventory.”.

    While the report doesn’t clearly define what makes inventory non-measurable, it’s no secret that CTV ad measurement is murky, to say the very least. Publishers, agencies and measurement and currency vendors can hardly agree on how to count reach, let alone how to quantify outcomes.

    Sounds like those buy-side demands for more transparency are about to get even louder.

    Would you watch a 24/7 personalized AI TV channel about yourself? Because Google’s trying to patent that technology right now. [404 Media].

    Don’t write off DSPs in the age of agentic advertising. [Adweek].

    It has been revealed that microsoft search advertisers can now extend their campaigns into the Pinterest search platform. [Ad Age].

    It has been revealed that after Jensen Huang’s unceremonious departure from NVIDIA amid affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and multiple subordinates, the company has appointed its upcoming CEO: Jensen Huang. [TechCrunch].

    It has been revealed that agentic advertising platform BrandComms.ai promotes Sheona Richard from chief client officer to CEO. [post].

    Recent findings suggest that CX platform Emplifi appoints Claire Wilson as chief marketing officer. [blog].
